turns.output: Every Sunday afternoon, my grandmother's kitchen filled with the savory perfume of vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, and bay leaves simmering together. That was how we knew chicken adobo was coming, and that the whole family would soon gather around her wooden table, hungry and happy. This recipe is hers, carried from Batangas to California in a notebook stained with decades of splatters and love. Adobo is often called the unofficial national dish of the Philippines, but in our home it was Lola's chicken: tender, glossy, salty, sour, and just a little sweet. She taught us that patience matters, that chicken should brown before it braises, and that no one leaves the table without rice for the sauce. I have made it for birthdays, heartbreaks, and Tuesdays. Now I am sharing it with you, hoping it brings your family the same comfort, conversation, and second helpings it has always brought mine.

Every family has one dish that brings everyone to the table without a single call, and for ours, it is chicken adobo. The moment garlic hits hot oil and vinegar begins to simmer with soy sauce, black peppercorns, and bay leaves, the whole house smells like home. My grandmother made it every Sunday, tasting the sauce with a spoon and adjusting it by memory alone. My mother learned by standing beside her, watching, stirring, and listening to stories that never made it into any cookbook. Now I make it for my own children, who argue over the last piece of chicken and spoon extra sauce over warm rice. This recipe is simple, forgiving, and deeply comforting, built on balance rather than strict rules. It is salty, tangy, savory, and just a little sweet. Make it once, taste as you go, and soon it will become part of your family story.

Imagine sunlight isn't just white — it's actually a mix of all the colors of the rainbow traveling together.

When that sunlight reaches Earth, it has to pass through our atmosphere, a blanket of air made of teeny-tiny molecules, much smaller than you can see. As the light bumps into these molecules, it gets scattered — bounced around in all directions. This is called Rayleigh scattering.

Here's the trick: different colors behave differently. Blue light has short, choppy waves, so it gets knocked around easily and scatters everywhere. Red, orange, and yellow light have longer, smoother waves, so they mostly sail straight through with less bouncing.

So during the day, blue light is scattered all over the sky above you. Whichever direction you look, some of that scattered blue light reaches your eyes, making the whole sky look blue.

At sunset, it's different. The sunlight has to travel through much more air to reach you, so most of the blue gets scattered away before it arrives. That leaves the reds and oranges behind — which is why sunsets look so fiery and beautiful!

Pretty cool, right? The sky isn't painted blue — it's light playing a bouncing game overhead!

Have you ever wondered why the sky looks blue instead of green or purple?

Sunlight looks white, but it is actually made of many colors mixed together, like a rainbow. You can see those colors when light passes through a prism or when a rainbow appears after rain.

Because blue light is scattered all over the sky, it reaches your eyes from every direction. Wherever you look up, you see that scattered blue light, so the whole sky appears blue.

At sunset, sunlight has to travel through more air to reach you. Most of the blue light gets scattered away before it arrives, leaving reds and oranges for you to enjoy.

When you visit a website, your browser has to download lots of files from the internet: text, images, logos, and code that tells the page how to look and behave. Downloading all of that takes time and data.

A browser cache is like a storage box on your computer where the browser keeps copies of some of those files after your first visit.

Next time you visit the same site, the browser checks its cache first. If it already has a recent copy of the logo, background image, or other files, it loads them instantly from your computer instead of downloading them again. This makes pages load much faster and uses less internet data.

Not everything is stored forever. Websites tell the browser how long to keep each file. Some files might be kept for a few hours, others for weeks. When a file expires, or the website updates it, the browser downloads a fresh copy and replaces the old one.

Sometimes the cache can cause problems, like showing an old version of a page. That's why you might hear advice to "clear your cache" — it empties the storage box, forcing the browser to download everything fresh.

When you visit a website, your browser has to download many files, such as images, logos, styles, and scripts. Downloading them takes time and uses data, especially on a slow connection.

A browser cache solves this problem by saving copies of some of those files on your own computer. Think of it like keeping a snack in your desk drawer instead of walking to a store every time you feel hungry.

The first time you visit a page, the browser downloads the files and stores them in the cache. The website can also tell the browser how long each file should be kept.

When you return to the same page later, the browser first checks its cache. If it finds a fresh copy of a file, it uses that copy right away instead of downloading it again. This makes the page load much faster and reduces the amount of data you use.

If a file is too old, missing, or has changed on the website, the browser downloads a new version and updates the cache.

Sometimes the cache can show an outdated page. Clearing the cache forces the browser to download everything fresh again.

The storm had taken the roof off the bothy and left Elias Venn with a kettle, a leaking oilskin, and a light that would not stay lit.

At dawn, when the wind finally dropped, he climbed down the iron steps to check the rocks for wreckage, as he had done every morning for twenty-three years on Skerry Holm. Gulls screamed. The sea sucked at black stone. Something was ringing.

Not a bell. Not the foghorn. A thin, bright trill, repeating.

Elias stopped with one boot in a pool. Wedged between two boulders below the tide line, half sunk in kelp, was a telephone. Not a mobile, lost from a yacht. A proper telephone, cream Bakelite, its cord trailing into the water like a vein, its dial intact. And it was ringing.

He should have left it. He should have reported it to the mainland, logged it, waited for instructions that would take three days to arrive by boat. Instead, because he had not heard another human voice since October, he lifted the receiver.

It was warm.

'Elias?' said a woman, clear as if she stood beside him. 'Don't let the light go out tonight. Whatever knocks, don't—'

The line died.

Thomas Hale had kept the light on Gull Rock for eleven years, and he knew every sound the island could make. Wind through the railings. Gulls crying before dawn. Waves striking stone in rhythm. He did not know the sound that woke him on Tuesday, thin and bright and wrong, repeating from somewhere below the tower.

He pulled on his coat, took his lantern, and climbed down the iron steps into the dark. The tide was low. Black rocks shone under a moon cut by cloud. The ringing came again, patient as a bell, from a pool between two boulders where the sea left its wreckage.

Thomas knelt. Among shells and rope and a drowned glove lay a telephone, dry inside a plastic case, its screen glowing green. No boat had landed. No supply ship was due for nine days. The nearest signal belonged to the mainland, twenty miles beyond rough water.

He lifted it with two fingers, as if it might bite. The ringing stopped. On the screen, white letters formed a line.

UNKNOWN CALLER

Then, beneath it, words appeared, though he had touched nothing.

PLEASE ANSWER, KEEPER. WE CAN SEE YOUR LIGHT.

Thomas looked up at the sea.

One year ago, I traded code reviews for career conversations — and learned more than I expected.

Here are 5 lessons from my first year as an engineering manager:

1. Your job is no longer to have the best solution. It's to create space for your team to find it.

2. 1:1s aren't status updates. They're where trust is built, blockers surface early, and people feel heard.

3. Context is kindness. Engineers don't resist decisions they understand — they resist decisions they don't.

4. Feedback delayed is feedback denied. Small, timely, and specific beats perfect and late.

5. You can't pour from an empty cup. Protecting my focus time made me a better manager, not a less available one.

I still miss building. But watching engineers grow, ship, and surprise themselves? That's the new build that matters.

To new managers: What surprised you most?

#EngineeringLeadership #Management

One year ago, I became an engineering manager. I thought the job was about having better technical answers. I was wrong.

Here are five lessons I learned:

1. Listening beats solving. My team rarely needed my solution first. They needed to feel heard, then space to think.

2. One on ones are the real work. Trust is built in small, consistent conversations, not big announcements.

3. Clear is kind. Vague feedback helped no one. Specific, timely, respectful feedback helped people grow.

4. Protect focus. My calendar became a team tool. Fewer meetings and clearer priorities gave engineers time to do deep work.

5. Let go of code. My value now comes from unblocking others, asking good questions, and creating clarity.

I still miss building things directly. But helping others build, grow, and succeed is even more rewarding.

Grateful for a team that taught me more than I taught them.

To new managers: What surprised you most?

#EngineeringManagement #Leadership

Jane Austen's *Pride and Prejudice* (1813) follows Elizabeth Bennet, the sharp-witted second of five daughters in a modest English family under pressure to marry well. When the wealthy Mr. Bingley rents a nearby estate, he falls for Elizabeth's sister Jane, while his proud friend Mr. Darcy clashes with Elizabeth. Misjudging Darcy as arrogant and believing false tales from the charming Wickham, Elizabeth rejects Darcy's first proposal. Darcy, meanwhile, must confront his own pride and class prejudice. Through letters, scandals — including Lydia Bennet's elopement — and Darcy's secret intervention to save the family's reputation, Elizabeth learns she misjudged him. Both change: Darcy becomes humbler and more generous, Elizabeth more self-aware. They eventually marry for love and mutual respect, as do Jane and Bingley.

Its themes include pride and prejudice as barriers to understanding, the rigid class hierarchy and economic necessity of marriage for women, reputation and propriety, and the tension between first impressions and true character. Austen satirizes a society that values wealth and status over integrity, while celebrating intelligence, moral growth, and marriages based on equality rather than convenience or passion alone. Ultimately, the novel suggests true love requires self-knowledge, humility, and willingness to see beyond social expectations and snap judgments.

Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice follows Elizabeth Bennet, the sharp and independent second daughter of a modest English family with five daughters and no son to inherit their estate. When the wealthy Mr. Bingley rents a nearby home, he falls for Elizabeth's gentle sister Jane, while his proud friend Mr. Darcy offends Elizabeth with his arrogance. Misjudgments multiply through gossip, family embarrassment, and the manipulations of the charming but dishonest Mr. Wickham. Elizabeth rejects Darcy's first proposal, angered by his interference in Jane's romance and his treatment of Wickham. Later, she learns the truth about Wickham's character and sees Darcy's quiet generosity, especially when he helps rescue her youngest sister from scandal. Both characters confront their flaws, Elizabeth her prejudice and Darcy his pride, and they eventually marry for love and respect.

The novel explores class, money, and marriage in a society where women depend on husbands for security. Austen satirizes snobbery and foolishness while valuing intelligence, integrity, and self knowledge. She shows that first impressions can mislead and that real worth lies beneath social rank. Through Elizabeth's growth, Austen argues that love should rest on understanding and character rather than wealth or appearance alone.

The printing press, developed by Johannes Gutenberg around 1440, changed Europe because it transformed how knowledge was produced, shared, and preserved.

Before printing, books were copied by hand, mainly by monks. They were rare, expensive, and took months or years to make, so literacy and learning were limited to clergy, nobles, and wealthy scholars. Movable type allowed hundreds of identical copies to be printed quickly and cheaply. By 1500, presses across Europe had produced millions of books—more than scribes had in the previous thousand years.

This abundance lowered the cost of education and helped spread literacy beyond elites. Standardized texts also made knowledge more reliable: scholars in different countries could read the same editions, compare ideas, correct errors, and build on each other's work. This accelerated the Renaissance, revived classical learning, and laid foundations for the Scientific Revolution.

Printing also weakened the Church's control over information. Martin Luther's pamphlets and translated Bibles spread rapidly, fueling the Protestant Reformation and religious wars, while encouraging people to interpret scripture themselves.

Finally, newspapers, pamphlets, and books in vernacular languages helped create shared national identities and public debate. In short, the press turned knowledge from a scarce privilege into a powerful, widely shared force that reshaped religion, science, politics, and society.

The printing press changed Europe because it transformed how knowledge was produced, shared, and preserved. Before its invention in the mid fifteenth century, books were copied by hand, mainly by monks and scribes. This process was slow, expensive, and prone to error, so books remained rare and confined to churches, universities, and wealthy elites. Johannes Gutenberg's movable type press made it possible to produce hundreds of copies in the time once needed for one manuscript. As presses spread to cities, the cost of books fell sharply and literacy became more valuable and more attainable.

Cheaper texts allowed ideas to travel faster and reach wider audiences. Religious reformers such as Martin Luther used printed pamphlets and Bibles to challenge church authority and encourage people to read scripture themselves, helping fuel the Reformation and religious division. Scholars could compare editions, share discoveries, and build on one another's work, which supported the Renaissance, the Scientific Revolution, and new standards of evidence. Governments, merchants, and ordinary readers also gained access to news, laws, maps, and practical manuals.

Printing weakened monopolies over knowledge, encouraged vernacular languages, and created a public sphere where debate could occur across distance. Europe moved toward a culture shaped by widespread reading, criticism, and cumulative learning.

Rain in San Francisco does not ruin a trip; it reveals a softer, moodier side of the city that sunny postcards rarely show. I started my morning in a cozy North Beach café, watching fog curl around Coit Tower while sipping a cappuccino and listening to rain tap the awning. From there, I ducked into City Lights Bookstore, browsing poetry between the puddles, then rode a cable car up slick, shining hills as droplets streaked the windows. By afternoon, the Ferry Building Marketplace felt inviting, filled with the smells of fresh sourdough, mushroom soup, and strong coffee. I sampled local cheeses, bought a handmade scarf, and watched ferries disappear into the gray bay. Later, I wandered through the de Young Museum in Golden Gate Park, where rain hammered the copper roof and the observation tower offered a misty panorama of treetops. For dinner, I found warmth in the Richmond District with a steaming bowl of clam chowder and garlic noodles, surrounded by locals shaking off umbrellas and laughing. Walking back to my hotel under a clearing sky, streets glistened gold beneath streetlights. San Francisco in the rain feels intimate, cinematic, and unforgettable, like discovering a secret version of a city.

Rain in San Francisco does not ruin a trip, it simply changes the rhythm and invites you to slow down and look closer at the city. I started my morning in a cozy cafe near Union Square, watching cable cars splash through shining streets while fog softened the tops of tall buildings. With a warm cup of coffee in hand, I wandered to the Ferry Building, where local bakers, flower sellers, and cheese makers filled the air with comforting smells. Outside, the bay looked silver and moody, and ferries disappeared into the mist like quiet ghosts. Later, I escaped the drizzle inside the California Academy of Sciences, where penguins waddled, butterflies floated through a rainforest dome, and children pressed their faces to aquarium glass. For lunch, I found clam chowder in a sourdough bowl at Fisherman's Wharf, eaten while rain tapped the windows and sea lions barked in the distance. The afternoon called for bookstores in North Beach, vinyl shops, and a slow ride through Chinatown, where red lanterns glowed against gray skies. By evening, the clouds lifted just enough for wet pavement to reflect neon lights, reminding me that San Francisco shines brightest after rain on days like this.

Tucked between a laundromat and a bookstore, Menya Kaze looks unassuming, but its ramen deserves serious attention. I ordered the tonkotsu, and the broth was extraordinary: rich, silky, deeply porky, with layers of garlic, ginger, and a gentle smoky finish that lingered pleasantly. The noodles were springy and perfectly cooked, the chashu melted instantly, and the ajitama egg had a jammy, seasoned yolk. Fresh scallions and wood ear mushrooms added brightness and crunch, balancing every spoonful beautifully.

Unfortunately, service tested my patience. We waited twenty minutes to be seated despite empty tables, another fifteen for water, and nearly forty for our bowls. Staff were polite but clearly overwhelmed, forgetful, and difficult to flag down for refills or the check.

Come for unforgettable broth, not efficiency. If you have time, patience, and nowhere urgent to be afterward, the flavor absolutely rewards the wait. I will return, cautiously, hungry, hopeful, and early.

Tucked on a quiet corner downtown, this small ramen shop delivers flavor that far outweighs its modest appearance. I ordered the tonkotsu, and the broth alone made the visit worthwhile. It was rich, silky, and deeply savory, with layers of pork flavor that lingered pleasantly after each spoonful. The noodles had a satisfying chew, the egg was perfectly jammy, and the chashu melted in my mouth. Fresh scallions and garlic oil added brightness without overpowering the bowl.

Service, however, tested my patience. We waited twenty minutes to be seated despite empty tables, then another thirty for our food. Our server was friendly but rarely checked in, and refills arrived only after repeated requests.

Still, I would return. Few places nearby achieve this level of depth and balance in a broth. Just come when you have time to spare, bring good company, and prepare to wait for something genuinely delicious indeed.

Remote work ultimately hurts junior engineers more than it helps them, despite its obvious comforts and flexibility. Early in a career, learning happens less through formal documentation or scheduled meetings and more through osmosis: overhearing senior engineers debug an outage, watching how they negotiate trade-offs in a design review, or asking a quick question without the friction of booking a call. Remote setups replace those spontaneous moments with Slack threads, delayed replies, and performative updates that reward visibility over curiosity. Juniors, who lack established networks and the confidence to interrupt, often suffer in silence, misinterpreting silence as competence expected rather than help needed. Mentorship also becomes transactional, limited to weekly one-on-ones instead of continuous feedback that builds judgment. While remote work can broaden access to jobs and eliminate commutes, it deprives newcomers of the social capital, tacit knowledge, and rapid feedback loops essential for growth. Companies can mitigate this with intentional pairing, recorded walkthroughs, and in-person onboarding, but few invest consistently. Until they do, junior engineers will trade short-term convenience for long-term stagnation, advancing more slowly and feeling less belonging than peers who learned shoulder to shoulder in an office during their most formative and impressionable professional years of development.

Remote work hurts junior engineers more than it helps them, even though its flexibility is appealing. Early in a career, learning happens less through training and more through constant, informal exposure to experienced colleagues. Junior engineers absorb judgment by overhearing design debates, watching seniors debug under pressure, asking questions without scheduling a meeting, and receiving immediate feedback on small mistakes before they become habits. Remote settings weaken each of these channels. A question that would take thirty seconds in person becomes a message that may sit unanswered for hours, so juniors either stall or guess. Code reviews become slower and more transactional, offering corrections without the reasoning that builds intuition. Mentorship also suffers because relationships rarely deepen through scheduled video calls alone, and managers cannot easily notice confusion, frustration, or disengagement through a screen. Remote work does offer real benefits, including no commute, wider job access, and quieter time for focused coding. Senior engineers with established networks and strong self direction can thrive under those conditions. Juniors, however, need proximity, spontaneity, and social belonging to grow quickly and confidently. Companies that insist on fully remote teams should therefore invest heavily in structured mentorship, pairing, and in person gatherings to compensate.

Running and swimming are both excellent aerobic exercises for staying fit, but they differ in impact, accessibility, and the muscles they develop.

Running is simple and convenient. It requires little more than good shoes and a safe route, making it easy to fit into a daily routine. It burns a high number of calories, strengthens bones through weight-bearing impact, and effectively builds endurance in the legs and core. However, that same impact can stress the knees, ankles, and hips, increasing injury risk, especially for beginners or people with joint problems. Weather and air quality can also limit outdoor running.

Swimming, by contrast, is low-impact because water supports the body's weight. This makes it gentler on joints while still providing a full-body workout for the arms, back, chest, legs, and core. It improves cardiovascular fitness, flexibility, and lung capacity, and is often recommended for rehabilitation and older adults. The main drawbacks are access and skill: it requires a pool or safe open water, may cost more, and proper technique takes time to learn.

Ultimately, running suits those seeking convenience and bone strength, while swimming suits those wanting joint-friendly, total-body conditioning. Combining both can offer balanced fitness and reduce overuse injuries.

Running and swimming are both excellent forms of aerobic exercise, but they suit different bodies, budgets, and preferences.

Running is simple and accessible. You need little more than supportive shoes and a safe route, and you can do it almost anywhere. It burns many calories in a short time, strengthens bones through repeated impact, and improves cardiovascular fitness and leg strength. It is also easy to track progress by distance, pace, or time. However, the impact can stress knees, ankles, and hips, especially on hard surfaces or with poor form. Weather, traffic, and safety can also limit when and where you run.

Swimming provides a full body workout that builds endurance, muscle tone, and lung capacity while placing very little stress on joints. The water supports your weight, making it ideal for people with arthritis, injuries, or higher body weight. It also keeps you cool and can feel relaxing. On the downside, swimming requires access to a pool or safe open water, which may cost money or require travel. Technique matters more, and some people dislike getting wet or find laps repetitive.

Ultimately, running offers convenience and intensity, while swimming offers low impact variety. The best choice is the one you enjoy and can repeat consistently.

1/5 Clever code feels brilliant when you write it. Simple code feels brilliant when you have to read, debug, and change it six months later.

You’ll spend 10x more time reading code than writing it — optimize for the reader.

2/5 Clever code shows how smart the author is. Simple code shows how much the author cares about the next person.

That next person is usually future you, tired, under pressure, and fixing a production bug.

3/5 Every clever trick adds hidden costs: more edge cases, harder onboarding, and code nobody wants to touch.

Simple code is boring and predictable — and in software, boring is reliable.

4/5 As Brian Kernighan said: “Debugging is twice as hard as writing code. If you write the cleverest code you can, you are, by definition, not smart enough to debug it.”

5/5 The goal isn’t the shortest one-liner. It’s code so obvious a new teammate can understand it in minutes.

Write for humans first, computers second. Simple wins.

1/5 Clever code feels great to write. Simple code feels great to read, debug, and change six months later. Guess which one your team does more often.

2/5 Simple code is easier to review. When logic is obvious, reviewers can spot real bugs instead of spending all their energy just trying to understand what the code does.

3/5 Simple code fails in simple ways. When something breaks at 2 a.m., you want clear logic you can follow step by step, not a puzzle that only its author can solve.

4/5 Simple code is easier to extend. New teammates can add features, fix edge cases, and refactor with confidence because they do not have to decode hidden tricks first.

5/5 Cleverness has a cost, and everyone after you pays it. Write the boring version. Your future self, your teammates, and your users will thank you.
